title: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), Louvre AO 5066
language: Moabite (Hebrew square script and transliteration, Compston 1919) / English (Compston 1919)
source: Louvre AO 5066 photograph (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0) + H. F. B. Compston's 1919 text and translation (public domain)
description: The Mesha Stele (c. 840 BCE), in which Mesha king of Moab tells of his revolt against Omri's house of Israel and names YHWH, line by line with Compston's 1919 text and translation and the photograph of the stele.
introduction:
The Mesha Stele, or Moabite Stone, is a black basalt stele set up about 840 BCE by Mesha, king of Moab, at Dibon (Dhiban in Jordan). In 34 lines of Moabite, written in the old Hebrew-Phoenician alphabet, Mesha says that Omri, king of Israel, and his son oppressed Moab because the god Chemosh was angry with his land, and that Chemosh then gave Mesha victory: he took Ataroth, Nebo and Jahaz from Israel and dragged 'the vessels of YHWH' before Chemosh, and he rebuilt the towns of his kingdom. It is the longest Iron Age inscription from the lands east of the Jordan and names Omri, Israel and the God of Israel. Its story runs parallel to the account of Mesha's revolt in the Old Testament, 2 Kings 3:4-27.

The stele was seen by the missionary F. A. Klein in 1868. Before it could be removed, a paper squeeze was taken for Charles Clermont-Ganneau, and in 1869 the stone was broken up by the local people. The larger pieces were recovered and are now in the Louvre (AO 5066), set in a plaster restoration based on the squeeze.

The text is H. F. B. Compston's edition of 1919 in Hebrew square letters, with his line-by-line English translation. Square brackets mark his restorations, overlined letters are uncertain, and dots in the English mark words lost at the broken end of the stele. Each section groups a few lines and shows the photograph of the whole inscribed face.
translator_notes: Compston's English is printed line for line with the stele, so words broken between lines are hyphenated as he prints them.

Each line is given in Compston's Hebrew square script (read right to left) and below it in a letter-for-letter Latin transliteration of that same text (ʾ b g d h w z ḥ ṭ y k l m n s ʿ p ṣ q r š t); the transliteration is mechanical and adds no reading of its own. · and | are the stele's word and sentence dividers; an overline marks a letter Compston gives as uncertain.

Compston: "Words in italics are required by English idiom: they are not in the original. Words and letters within square brackets are restored conjecturally. Words within curved brackets are alternative renderings."
Compston's note: lines 4, 7. "Look upon," i.e., with exultation over a fallen foe. Cf. Ps. lix. 10 E.V.
Compston's note: line 16. I.e., recognised settlers. Cf. 2 Sam. i. 13.
Compston's note: line 21. See note, line 3.
Compston's note: lines 24, 25. See note, line 3.
Compston's note: line 30. See 2 Kings iii. 4.
